settings.vibe: CRT glow, mall food courts, dial-up patience

concept.summary: Miles Okada, a present-day AI startup founder, wakes up in his fourteen-year-old body in 1996 — and discovers the time-travel fantasy is a lie. He can't predict a single game score. He doesn't remember which stocks matter or when anything happens. The only future knowledge that survived the trip is the stuff he actually loved at fourteen: every Tupac and Biggie track-listing, every movie twist, decades of pop-culture trivia. When his three best friends finally believe him, they appoint themselves his management team — and every scheme they invent to monetize a psychic fourteen-year-old is stupid, physically impossible, illegal, or socially fatal, because they are fourteen, have eleven dollars between them, and need to be home by dinner. And then there's the thread nobody can know about: Ms. Vann, the young student teacher Miles worshipped from the back row the first time he was fourteen. Now he can actually TALK to her — book recommendations, dry jokes about the faculty, the kind of easy adult rapport that makes her linger by his desk — and every one of those conversations is a live grenade: he is a grown man in a child's seat, she has no idea, and there is no version of this that isn't wrong.
themes: a connection that must never be one

characters.name: Miles Okada
characters.backstory: 35-year-old AI startup founder whose consciousness wakes in his 14-year-old body, 1996. Future knowledge is nearly useless: no scores, no stocks, no dates — only rap track-listings, movie twists, pop trivia.
characters.motivations: Prove his knowledge is worth something; find one scheme that works.
characters.flaws: Pitches like a founder to people with five-dollar net worths; needs the future to matter.
characters.need: To be fourteen with his friends instead of performing an adult.
characters.arc: From monetizing the future to being present.

relationships.description: best friend since second grade — self-appointed manager
friend — the muscle who has never won a fight
friend — the 'numbers guy' who is failing pre-algebra
his young English teacher — an impossibly mature rapport HE experiences as adult conversation; ethically impossible and he knows it

characters.name: Reggie Park
characters.backstory: First believer; read one Forbes at the orthodontist and now speaks in percentages he invents.
characters.motivations: Manage Miles to their mutual fortune; be somebody's boss.
characters.flaws: Confidence fully decoupled from competence; doubles every failed bet.
characters.need: To be a good friend, which is free.
characters.arc: From manager of a psychic to friend of a weird kid.

relationships.description: client and best friend — the asset

characters.name: Tone DeLuca
characters.backstory: Biggest kid in ninth grade, softest heart in the county; cries at long-distance commercials.
characters.flaws: Agrees to everything, executes nothing on schedule.
characters.need: To learn size isn't the job.

relationships.description: the psychic he'd take a punch for

characters.name: P-Dub Watts
characters.backstory: Keeps the crew's 'books' in a Trapper Keeper; failing pre-algebra with visible pride.
characters.motivations: Track the money there isn't any of.
characters.flaws: Precision about fictional numbers, allergy to real ones.

relationships.description: the CEO he invoices in gum

characters.name: Ms. Vann
characters.backstory: 24, first year teaching ninth-grade English; earnest and lonely in a way that makes a student who talks like an equal disorienting.
characters.motivations: Be taken seriously as a teacher; have one conversation a day that isn't about hall passes.
characters.flaws: Poor boundary-setting with a kid who flatters her with book recommendations; mistakes a 35-year-old's performance for kinship.
characters.need: Boundaries that don't need to be interesting.

relationships.description: her student — the rapport is impossibly mature and she cannot place why

guardrails.mustPreserve: The uselessness of Miles's future knowledge (no scores, no stocks, no dates — only rap, movie twists, pop trivia); the friends-as-terrible-management-team engine; the Ms. Vann subplot as ethically uncomfortable dark comedy.
guardrails.avoid: Nostalgia-listicle humor (jokes that are just "remember Tamagotchis?"); any scheme that actually works; adults who take a fourteen-year-old's pitch seriously without cost.
guardrails.doNotTurnInto: Back to the Future with a sports almanac (get-rich time-travel plot); a peer-romance coming-of-age story; a fix-the-timeline mission.
guardrails.toneGuardrails: Affectionate toward 1996, merciless toward Miles's dignity. Dark where the premise is dark (a 35-year-old mind in a kid's life), never mean toward the kids themselves.
guardrails.edgeNotes: The Ms. Vann dynamic is deliberately uncomfortable: an adult mind's impossibly mature rapport with a young teacher, played as dark comedy of impossibility. The discomfort is the point — keep it on the page as discomfort.
guardrails.sensitiveHandling: Ms. Vann never reciprocates romantically; boundaries hold; the comedy comes from social danger and consequence, never from the relationship progressing.
guardrails.uniqueness: Time-slip comedy where future knowledge is mostly WORTHLESS — the engine is competence colliding with a fourteen-year-old's total lack of leverage.
guardrails.referencePriorities: Freaks and Geeks texture over high-concept time-travel plotting; Big's body-logic honesty for the adult-mind-kid-world gap.
